title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Water Utilities | PT
description: Dye penetrant inspection of stainless piping, pumps, valves and aluminum covers for US water and wastewater plants. Crews travel to your site. Get a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Water and Wastewater Utilities
html:
Liquid penetrant testing for water and wastewater utilities in the United States is how surface-breaking cracks are found on equipment a magnet cannot examine: stainless chemical feed piping, reverse osmosis skids, pump casings and impellers, bronze valve bodies, aluminum dome and cover welds, and stainless weirs and baffles. Atlantis mobilizes SNT-TC-1A qualified technicians to your plant, pump station or tank site, and returns a report with each indication sketched. To scope the work, request a dye penetrant inspection quote.

Why penetrant suits treatment plants

A treatment plant uses far more nonmagnetic material than a tank farm. Chemical feed lines carry sodium hypochlorite, ferric chloride, caustic, fluoride and polymer, and they are built from stainless steel, nickel alloys or lined carbon steel. Membrane and desalination systems run high-pressure duplex and super duplex piping in salty water. Aluminum covers and domes protect clarifiers and tanks. None of this can carry a magnetic field, and penetrant needs only a clean surface and a crack open to it.

That is both the strength and the limit. Penetrant cannot see a crack under a coating, a closed flaw, or any wall loss. For thickness questions use the UT page for water utilities, and for cracks in carbon steel welds on tanks and pipe the MT page is usually quicker.

Chemical feed systems and process piping

Sodium hypochlorite and ferric chloride are aggressive to many stainless grades, and chloride exposure can drive crevice attack and chloride stress corrosion cracking in austenitic stainless. API 571 describes chloride cracking as fine, branched surface-initiated cracking, and welds, heat-affected zones and cold-formed bends are the first places to look. A penetrant examination of those welds after a leak, after weld repair or at a planned outage gives the plant a clear record of what is open to the surface.

Fabricated spools, tank nozzles and skid connections get penetrant examination during construction and repair as well. Each weld is identified by the number the contractor assigns, the examination points follow the repair procedure, and the report links indications to those identifiers. We do not write welding procedures; the contractor and engineer do.

Membrane skids, UV reactors and ozone contactors

High-pressure feed piping for reverse osmosis uses duplex and super duplex stainless to resist chloride attack, and the welds are small, controlled and sensitive to heat input. UV reactor shells and ozone contactor piping are stainless as well. Penetrant examination of those welds is a common acceptance activity on new work and a diagnostic tool after a leak.

The welds are often tight and inside skids with little room, so lighting and access shape the quality of the examination. We plan the scope with the skid drawings, and where a weld cannot be reached for cleaning, developing and viewing, the report lists it as not examined with the reason.

Pumps, valves and aluminum structures

Pump casings, impellers and valve bodies in stainless, bronze or other alloys are examined after weld repair, machining or buildup. Wastewater pumps in abrasive or corrosive service wear unevenly, and a repaired area needs to be shown free of surface cracks before it returns to service. We identify each part by serial number and record the surface condition.

Aluminum geodesic domes and covers over tanks and clarifiers are welded or bolted structures, and welded aluminum joints crack at heat-affected zones under fatigue or thermal cycling. Penetrant is the usual way to examine them. Because aluminum surfaces are soft, grinding smears metal across small flaws, and the procedure may require a light etch or another cleaning step before examination.

Materials, contaminants and drinking-water contact

Penetrant materials used on austenitic stainless steel and nickel-base alloys are controlled for halogen and sulfur content. ASME Section V Article 6 requires that control, and the report records the manufacturer, batch number and certification for the penetrant, remover and developer. Materials from carbon steel work are kept separate from those used on stainless.

Equipment that touches potable water needs cleanliness after examination. Penetrant, remover and developer are removed by wiping or flushing as the procedure states, and the utility decides whether the cleaning and the later disinfection are sufficient for return to service. For a wastewater process the same discipline applies, because penetrant carried into a biological process is something the plant wants to avoid.

Technique details for plant conditions

  • Penetrant system. Solvent removable visible dye is the usual site choice. Fluorescent penetrants add sensitivity where a dark area and ultraviolet light can be arranged. ASTM E165 and Article 6 define the methods.
  • Surface preparation. Remove scale, oil, paint, scale from hypochlorite crystals and spatter. Wet surfaces must be dried completely, because water blocks entry of the penetrant.
  • Temperature. Without a qualified procedure, work stays within roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit at the surface. Cold buildings and sun-baked roofs both fall outside that range at times, and the procedure sets how we respond.
  • Dwell time and developer. Times come from the procedure and the material, and the technician records them for each examination.
  • Lighting. A stated minimum light level at the surface for visible dye, and a dark enclosure with a measured UV intensity for fluorescent work.
  • Verification. Where the procedure requires it, system performance is checked on a comparison block at the start of work.

Codes, regulators and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 govern the method. Depending on the asset, the utility's specification may cite AWWA D100 for tanks, AWWA C200 for steel pipe, or ASME B31.3 for process piping in treatment plants. The Safe Drinking Water Act frames the regulatory context for public water systems, and states enforce it. The acceptance criteria are the ones named in the construction specification, and the engineer of record decides what to do with a relevant indication. Atlantis does not calculate remaining life, set intervals or decide fitness for service. Our guide to Article 6 explains the code basis.

When PT is the wrong choice

Penetrant versus other methods for utility equipment
SituationBetter methodWhy
Stainless chemical feed weldPTNot magnetic, flaw open to the surface
Carbon steel tank weldMTFaster on ferromagnetic steel
Wall loss in pipe or tankUTPenetrant shows no thickness
Porous cast housingCase by casePenetrant bleeds from pores and masks cracks
Crack beneath coating or liningNot PTNeeds removal of the barrier first

Classifying indications on utility equipment

Penetrant produces linear bleed-out from cracks, rounded bleed-out from porosity, and non-relevant indications from geometry such as a sharp weld toe, a machined edge or a thread root. On stainless welds, light surface staining from pickling or heat tint can also confuse a reader. The technician classifies each indication, re-cleans and re-develops a doubtful one where the procedure allows, and records which were re-examined. The distinction matters to the utility, because a relevant indication triggers an engineering decision and a non-relevant one does not.

When a plant shares examination records with a regulator or an insurer, a clear separation between what was observed and what was decided protects everyone. Our reports keep the observation, the classification and the acceptance call as three separate entries, and the acceptance call refers to the criteria named in the scope.

What the report contains

Each report identifies the component and weld, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system with batch numbers and certification references, the dwell and developing times, surface temperature, surface preparation, and the technician name and SNT-TC-1A level. Indications are drawn on a sketch with location, size and type, accept or reject is recorded against the named criteria, and an ASNT Level III reviews the report. Areas that could not be examined, and why, appear in the summary.

What to send for a quote

  • List of welds, parts or skids with drawings and identifiers
  • Material grades: stainless type, duplex, nickel alloy, aluminum, bronze
  • Governing specification and acceptance criteria, plus any limits on halogen and sulfur
  • Process chemicals touching the equipment and any residue limits
  • Surface condition, coating, insulation and who cleans the surface
  • Temperature, indoor or outdoor work, and lighting conditions
  • Access, entry permits, security requirements and site address

Scheduling around plant operations

Penetrant work sits late in a repair or fabrication sequence, after grinding and before coating, so it depends on other trades finishing. Tanks, wet wells and large vaults are confined spaces under 29 CFR 1910.146 and your permit program, and chemical rooms add their own lockout and chemical-residue steps. Atlantis technicians travel to your site with penetrant systems, light meters and a UV lamp, and the plant provides power, access, permits and escort where required.

Training your own plant technicians in PT

Maintenance teams that repair pumps and fabricate spools may want their own surface examiners. PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training follow SNT-TC-1A, and the penetrant testing simulator supports practice before live parts. Your utility certifies its own personnel under a written practice, and written practice development helps put one in place. The MT versus PT comparison helps with choosing a method, and the national page is penetrant testing.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US, does not run in-line tools through pipelines, and does not decide whether a cracked part may stay in service. For weld work beyond PT, see weld inspection, and for procedure writing see procedure development.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done on stainless steel chemical feed piping?
faq.a: Yes. Stainless is not magnetic, so penetrant is the standard surface method. We use materials controlled for halogen and sulfur content, and we report each weld by its identifier so the plant can trace results.

faq.q: Will penetrant testing find leaks or wall loss?
faq.a: No. It shows only cracks and pores open to the surface. A leak path may be visible as an indication if it reaches the surface, but thickness loss needs an ultrasonic survey, which can be scoped alongside in one mobilization.

faq.q: How do you protect drinking water after penetrant work?
faq.a: Penetrant, remover and developer are wiped or flushed away as the procedure states, and the utility decides whether cleanliness and later disinfection are adequate before the equipment returns to potable service.

faq.q: Can you examine aluminum domes and covers?
faq.a: Yes. Welded aluminum joints crack at heat-affected zones under thermal or fatigue loading, and penetrant is the usual method. Grinding smears soft metal over flaws, so the procedure may call for a light etch first.

faq.q: What surface conditions are a problem for PT?
faq.a: Wet surfaces, scale, oil, paint, spatter and rough or porous castings. Penetrant cannot enter a flaw it cannot reach and bleeds out of pores, so the report marks any area where surface condition prevented a clear result.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects penetrant indications?
faq.a: The construction specification gives the criteria, and the utility's engineer of record decides repair or acceptance. Atlantis records each indication with location, size and type against the criteria you provide.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote PT at a treatment plant?
faq.a: A list of welds or parts with drawings, material grades, governing specification, process chemicals, surface condition, temperature, access arrangements, entry permits and site security steps. That is enough to scope the examination.

faq.q: Do you work indoors in chemical rooms?
faq.a: Yes, when the plant has isolated the equipment, cleared chemical residue and issued the permit. Visible dye needs adequate lighting, and fluorescent work needs a darkened area, which we plan with the plant.

faq.q: Is liquid penetrant testing allowed in cold weather?
faq.a: Within the temperature range in the procedure, roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit at the surface, unless a procedure is qualified for other temperatures. Outside that range the part is warmed or enclosed, or the examination waits.
